title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A segment is only real when you can name its customer, its invoice and its margin.
epigraph.author: Underwriting Rule

web_blocks.html: MPS reports three market-facing segments. The audited segment note (Note 36 of the FY26 consolidated statements) gives each one a revenue line, a segment result, depreciation and employee cost [1]. In FY26 consolidated revenue from operations was ₹768.37 Cr (+5.71%). EBITDA was ₹235.85 Cr (a 30.7% margin) and profit after tax was ₹173.22 Cr [1]. Behind that single line sit three very different businesses. Research Solutions is ₹463.51 Cr (60.3% of revenue). Education Solutions is ₹208.90 Cr (27.2%). Corporate Learning is ₹95.95 Cr (12.5%) [1]. The MD&A rounds those shares to 60%, 27% and 13%. The shares used in this chapter are computed from the ₹ lakh figures in Note 36. Management calls the common platform an ‘engine’ of content engineering, platform technology and AI [1]. What changes from segment to segment is who pays, for which unit of work, and how much of the unit’s value MPS keeps.

web_blocks.html: A note on how to read the profit columns. Segment result in Note 36 is struck before interest and before ₹29.31 Cr of net unallocated corporate cost [1]. On that basis Research produced ₹170.24 Cr of the ₹258.77 Cr total (65.8%), Education ₹77.22 Cr (29.8%) and Corporate Learning ₹11.31 Cr (4.4%), all computed from the note. Corporate Learning is an eighth of revenue and under a twentieth of segment profit; Research is 60% of revenue and about two-thirds of profit. The quality of this company is therefore mostly the quality of Research Solutions. Education is the growth engine and Corporate Learning is the repair job.

Segment 1: Research Solutions. The annual report describes it as AI-first knowledge solutions across the research lifecycle. That covers content and data transformation, research integrity and verification, author and editorial solutions, and platform-based hosting, workflow and analytics [1]. In practice there are five sub-businesses. First, journals production turns accepted manuscripts into finished articles. Second, scholarly books: management said it secured a multi-year commitment for 900 titles in FY26 [1]. Third, platforms. DigiCore and DigiCorePro handle production workflow. DigiCore launched at the Frankfurt Book Fair in 2012, is modular and open-source-based, and MPS uses it for its own production. Other platforms are MPSTrak (workflow tracking), THINK365 (subscription and order management), mag+ (mobile publishing) and ScholarStor. ScholarlyStats and MPSInsight provide usage analytics. HighWire is the Stanford-born hosting platform acquired in 2020 [26, 27, 1]. Platforms were 28.56% of consolidated revenue in FY25 by the CFO’s count [20]. Fourth, author services through AJE. MPS bought AJE from Springer Nature in February 2024, together with the Curie AI tool and Research Quality Evaluation, for US$8.40 million (₹69.67 Cr) [1]. Fifth, pre-acceptance services: the Journal Editorial Office and peer-review management that management says scaled because of AJE [25].

Worked example (Research): a top-five publisher hands over peer review and production. On the Q2 FY27 call, Christine Miranda said one of the five largest companies in the market is moving more than 110,000 submissions a year onto MPS’s peer-review platform. She said one of MPS’s biggest customers also gave it a large new production mandate plus a research-integrity mandate [2]. The customer is not named. The single customer worth 17.3% of group revenue in the audited note is also unnamed. We should not assume they are the same client [1]. The publisher’s problem is throughput. Paper mills and machine-written manuscripts are arriving in unprecedented numbers. As Rahul Arora (Chairman and CEO) put it on that call, ‘volume is not the issue, throughput is the issue’ [2]. What the publisher buys is a bundle of units. One is a screened, reviewed and decided submission. The other, for accepted papers, is a finished article. The build runs in steps. Submissions land in a peer-review system that MPS operates and staffs. Research Integrity Check sits on top of DigiCore. It flags paper-mill signatures, identity fraud and image manipulation before an editor spends time [25]. Editors and reviewers are assigned and chased by MPS coordinators. Accepted manuscripts then enter production. DigiXML converts them to structured formats, and AI-enabled composition and quality checks run. The Q1 FY27 call describes one-touch workflows, automated alt-text for accessibility and AI checks that catch errors before proofs. The output flows to a hosting platform such as HighWire or DigiCorePro [25, 26]. The price unit is the outcome: a submission handled or an article made ready. It is billed under a contract that the CEO says typically runs ‘three to five years’ [2]. The customer sees faster decisions and clean articles at a volume its own staff could not reach. The audited note shows how this reaches the P&L. Research employee cost fell from ₹185.13 Cr to ₹160.36 Cr in FY26 (computed from Note 36). Segment revenue rose 1.0% and the segment margin climbed [1].

Worked example (Research): an author buys help, and the publisher pays for the outcome. AJE sells straight to researchers off a price list. English-language editing starts at $13, scientific editing at $420, presubmission review at $289 and the Curie writing assistant at $11.25 a month. AJE says it has served more than a million authors in 192 countries [28]. The author uploads a manuscript. An editor matched to the field returns tracked changes and a report. The author then submits to the target journal. Since April 2026 AJE also sells pre-submission peer review. Christine Miranda called it the first genuinely new service in more than two years [25]. Management describes a mechanical change. Plain language editing is being absorbed by AI, through the Rubriq engine built on more than one million expert edits. AJE is therefore steering authors toward integrity and quality work, and toward being paid for results [1, 25]. The headline claim is a ‘manuscript acceptance rate of roughly 52% against an industry baseline near 32%’ in controlled work [25]. That comparison is management’s own data and has not been audited. Acceptance rates vary sharply by journal tier. We treat the claim as a sales argument rather than a measured moat.

What is weak in Research. First, reported growth was only 1.0% in FY26 because AJE was deliberately shrunk. Excluding AJE the segment grew about 17% [1]. Second, geography moved sharply. Research revenue from US customers fell 20.6% and from China 25.0%. Europe rose 26.8% and the rest of the world more than doubled (all computed from Note 43). That is consistent with the AJE author base in the US and China giving way to publisher work billed in Europe [1]. Third, dependence. One customer is 17.3% of group revenue and the top 15 are 58.05%. Management describes the large-publisher relationships as the heart of Research [1, 2]. Fourth, the publishers are building competing tools. Springer Nature developed a nonsense-text detector, an image checker (Snappshot) and an irrelevant-reference checker in-house. It donated the first to the STM Integrity Hub, so screening technology can reach the industry for free [29]. COPE’s forum also records that no AI-detection tool is 100% accurate. It adds that detectors cannot keep pace with new AI [30]. MPS’s answer is that it sits inside the production and review workflow and sells throughput, not detection alone. That is plausible. But detection by itself is a capability a large publisher can pull in-house.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: One profit pool, three different businesses
paragraphs: Put the segment note next to the call transcripts and one thing stands out. Research earns about 65.8% of segment profit, so when someone tells you MPS is a three-legged stool, they are being kind. It is one strong leg, one fast-growing leg whose newest component is lower-margin, and one leg being rebuilt.

That is not a criticism. A business with a 36.7% segment result margin in its main segment, and reported EBITDA margins of 45.1% and 48.2% there in the last two quarters, can carry a weak third segment for a long time. It does mean the diligence questions are narrow: how durable are the big-publisher contracts, and how much of each AI efficiency gain does the customer take back at renewal?

web_blocks.html: Segment 2: Education Solutions. The annual report defines it as AI-led learning content and knowledge solutions. These cover content development, multi-platform digital delivery, accessibility and learning platforms for education companies, ed-tech and continuing-education providers and academic institutions. Clinical knowledge now joins them through Unbound Medicine [1]. Inside the segment sit the OWL (‘One With Learning’) global education practice, learning services such as accessibility, translation and digital transformation, and Unbound [8, 1]. FY26 revenue rose 36.3% to ₹208.90 Cr, or about 29% excluding Unbound. Unbound added ₹11.78 Cr in its first 49 days [1]. The segment result margin edged up from 35.7% to 37.0% (computed). Geography is the key risk marker. 79.0% of Education revenue came from US customers in FY26 (computed from Note 43) [1]. In the first half of FY27 revenue grew 36% and EBITDA grew 14.5%. Education reached 30.6% of group revenue against 27.2% a year earlier. Unbound contributed ₹41.6 Cr in the half [2]. Unbound was bought for US$16.5 million on 9 February 2026. It had a run-rate of about US$800,000 a month by mid-2026. The CFO put its margins at 18% to 20%, up from 12% to 13% at purchase [1, 25, 2].

Worked example (Education): a nursing school subscribes to Nursing Central. The customer is an archetype rather than a named client. Think of a US or Canadian nursing programme or medical school, Unbound’s core institutional base [18, 31]. The problem is producing ‘practice-ready’ nurses with trustworthy references at the point of need. The product is an annual institutional subscription to Nursing Central. Unbound describes it as unifying clinical references, curriculum resources and teaching tools. Unbound Scenarios adds case-based clinical-judgement training, and AI Assist helps build teaching material. The references come from partners that include Johns Hopkins Medicine and Oxford University Press, both of which appear on Unbound’s own news page [32]. Delivery is a hosted platform and mobile apps rather than a project team. The CEO says Unbound is 35 people delivering about US$9 million of revenue [25]. It is priced per institution per year, with group discounts. Rahul Arora says that ‘every renewal with a customer, whether it’s a 10-year-old customer or a three-year-old customer, has a price increase’ [25, 32]. Unbound’s own release cites a 97% annual institutional renewal rate [31]. Billing is in advance. Unbound brought ₹34.98 Cr of contract liabilities (deferred revenue) onto MPS’s balance sheet at acquisition [1]. The customer sees an app its students and faculty use every day. MPS sees a renewal base. The AI answer layer is built on open large language models over a walled garden of licensed, peer-reviewed content. The moat is therefore the licensed content and clinical editorial process, not the model [25].

Worked example (Education): a K-12 publisher meets a state adoption deadline. The archetype is a US school publisher whose programme is up for a state adoption. One example is the Florida mathematics cycle that led Q2 FY27 bookings, with California to follow [2]. The publisher needs student and teacher materials, world-language editions and accessible versions by a fixed date. The CEO noted that accessibility rules stay on the books with compliance deadlines [2]. MPS’s education teams author or rework content and convert it to structured formats. They build accessible versions (EPUB, alt-text, remediation), translate and localise, and run quality assurance. AI sits in every step. The CEO said on the Q2 FY26 call that more than 60% of Education’s growth came from AI-powered workflows. He also said ‘the climb from 31% to 36% is all automation and AI’ [17]. Pricing is project-based, usually fixed-price recognised on percentage of completion, or unit-priced production. The revenue policy in the annual report names both [1]. The publisher sees a compliant package arrive faster. The economics depend on how much of the AI saving the publisher takes back in price.

What is weak in Education. Three things stand out. The first is lumpiness. The US adoption calendar drives bookings. Revenue growth slowed to 11.3% in Q3 FY26 after 52.4% in Q2 and 56.64% in Q1. Management called the dip a one-off [18, 17, 10]. The second is deflation. AI makes content production cheaper, so the same revenue needs less effort. An analyst on the Q2 FY27 call said organic growth in Education is ‘not very exciting’ once the acquisition is stripped out [2]. The third is mix. Unbound carries a lower margin than project work. That is the likeliest reason H1 EBITDA grew 14.5% against 36% revenue growth, after a 35.1% Q1 margin. We have not seen the Q2 segment table, so we do not put a number on Q2’s margin [2, 25]. Customer budgets in US schools and universities also depend on state and federal funding. Management spent part of the Q2 FY27 call on how US appropriations affect Unbound, nursing programmes and school districts [2].

Segment 3: Corporate Learning. The annual report defines it as technology-enabled workforce and enterprise learning. That means custom learning design and content, simulation and immersive (AR/VR) learning, and learning platforms and consulting, for corporates, government agencies and institutions [1]. The entities are MPS Interactive Systems (the former Tata Interactive Systems, acquired 2018), MPS Europa in Baar, Switzerland, and EI Design (2022). Others are Liberate Learning in Australia (2023, including App-eLearn Pty Ltd) and TOPSIM, the German business-simulation house in Tübingen [24, 1, 33]. The MPS site lists custom eLearning with gamification, simulation and animation, micro-learning and mobile learning. It also lists experience-centre and experiential learning design, consulting and learning platforms [34]. FY26 revenue fell 16.5% to ₹95.95 Cr. The segment result fell from ₹20.00 Cr to ₹11.31 Cr (margin 11.8% against 17.4%) [1]. The cleanup was structural. Liberate became wholly owned on 28 October 2025, releasing ₹15.73 Cr of deferred-consideration liability as exceptional income. MPS Europa is being folded under MPS Interactive. Rodney Beach, Liberate’s former promoter, became segment president [1, 17]. By year end MPS Interactive’s quarterly EBITDA margin was above 29%, and the segment returned to growth in Q4 FY26 [1]. In Q1 FY27 revenue was ₹27.60 Cr (+6.9%) at a 25.3% EBITDA margin, against 16.9% a year earlier, on a headcount about 33% lower. In the first half the margin was about 25% against about 16%. EBITDA rose 77% with 19% fewer people [25, 2].

Worked examples (Corporate Learning): a bank’s legacy training estate, and a German simulation. The first customer is an archetype: a large Australian bank or retailer, the kind of account Liberate serves. Management has mentioned a large banking customer and a major Australian retailer in AI-partnership work without naming either [8, 20]. The problem is thousands of legacy courses sitting in an LMS, LXP and SharePoint, disconnected from job performance. What gets bought is a programme, not a course. Soma Bhaduri described it on the Q1 FY27 call as role-based learning rebuilt from the legacy assets, AI chatbots for operational queries, multilingual delivery through the BridgeAI translation engine, and simulations [25]. Designers audit the estate. AI-assisted authoring, translation and quality checks compress production time. Media and development work is flexed through a gig and associate network instead of fixed staff [25]. It is billed as a fixed-price project on percentage of completion or as a managed learning service. The customer-visible outcome is performance at work rather than completion certificates. One verified data point shows how such deals grow. An invitation to join a conglomerate’s supplier panel turned into work above US$1 million plus a US$850,000 experience-centre project, per the Q1 FY26 call [10]. The second example is TOPSIM. A German industrial or retail group, such as the customers named on TOPSIM’s site (Kärcher, EDEKA, Vorwerk, Heidelberg Cement), licenses a business simulation for a leadership programme of ‘10 or 1000 people’. It is delivered classroom, blended or online on TOPSIM’s cloud platform [35]. Pricing is not disclosed. Management said in Q2 FY25 that TOPSIM’s top ten customers were under 40% of its revenue. It also said TOPSIM would pay its first dividend to MPS from FY25 [8].

What is weak in Corporate Learning. It lost 16.5% of its revenue and 43% of its segment result in FY26 (₹20.00 Cr to ₹11.31 Cr, computed). Its employee cost is still 46.8% of segment revenue, up from 44.3% (computed from Note 36). And its market is growing faster than it is. Rahul Arora told the Q1 FY27 call the corporate market grows 12% to 13% while MPS grew 6% to 7%. He called it ‘the area where a lot of the catch-up has to happen’ [25]. The headcount cuts and the move to gig delivery are cost fixes. Soma Bhaduri herself said ‘this is not a recovery of the legacy business’. She described a repositioning from learning creation to enterprise capability enablement [25]. The annual report records a ₹12.93 Cr goodwill impairment in FY26 exceptionals without attributing it to a segment [1]. The segment president called enterprise demand ‘patchy’ in Q3 FY26 [18]. Our judgment is that Corporate Learning has stopped losing ground on margin. Until it shows growth near its 12% goal with margins near its 30% steady-state goal for several quarters, treat it as an option on a turnaround, not a pillar [25].

web_blocks.html: Client concentration. The audited note discloses one customer at ₹133.17 Cr, or 17.33% of FY26 revenue (18.59% in FY25). Revenue from the top 15 customers was ₹446.00 Cr, or 58.05% (61.09% in FY25). No other customer reached 10% [1]. Management’s quarterly disclosures give a finer view. They do not always agree with the audited note, because the basis differs (quarterly against annual, clients billed excluding B2C customers). The CFO told the Q2 FY27 call that ‘our top five clients fell to 46% of revenue from 51%’. The client count had also risen sharply, which mostly reflects Unbound’s institutional subscribers rather than new project clients [2, 25]. The direction is toward lower concentration. But with about half of revenue from five clients, the business is still exposed to a single procurement decision.

web_blocks.html: What ‘AI-first’ and ‘paid for outcomes’ mean mechanically. The old production price was a rate per page, per article or per hour. Each hour saved by tooling was an hour not billed. The customer’s procurement team used the saving to ask for a lower rate at renewal. In the model management describes, MPS prices the finished unit. That could be an article made ready, a submission reviewed, an accessible title delivered or a subscription renewed. The saving is then divided between price and margin. Rahul Arora’s words: ‘Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume, and that’s where the margin kind of comes from’ [2]. In the Q4 FY25 call he said benefits are ‘shared fairly equally between the customer and us’ [20]. Management says 25% of revenue now comes from outcome-based partnerships and 45% from recurring themes [25]. Those are unaudited operating metrics without a published definition. The audited signal is the cost line. Group employee benefits expense fell 2.4% while revenue rose 5.7%. Research employee cost fell 13.4% (computed). Research’s EBITDA margin before unallocated costs rose from about 36.8% to 39.9% (computed). It then reached 45.1% and 48.2% in Q1 and Q2 FY27 [1, 25, 2]. MPS also capitalises almost no development spend (₹0.21 Cr of intangible assets under development in FY26). The work of MPS Labs, about 250 to 300 people, therefore runs through the P&L [1, 17]. What we cannot see is the rate card. Whether the price per unit has fallen, and by how much, is not disclosed.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: Separate the audited from the narrated
paragraphs: Every segment in this chapter has two layers of evidence. The audited layer is the segment note: revenue, result, depreciation, employee cost, geography, customer concentration. The narrated layer is the call: segment EBITDA margins, ‘outcome-based’ revenue shares, acceptance rates, run-rates, pipeline.

The narrated layer has been accurate where we could cross-check it: the Q1 FY27 growth rates the segment heads quoted (+13.2%, +42.2%, +6.9%) reproduce exactly from the Q1 FY26 presentation and the Q1 FY27 figures. It is still the part of the story where definitions are chosen by the speaker, which is why we lean on the audited layer for conclusions and use the narrated layer for direction.

web_blocks.html: What would change our view of segment quality (business triggers only). The first trigger is Research ex-AJE growth below about 10% for two consecutive quarters while margins keep rising. That would suggest price give-back is outrunning volume. The second is a top-five publisher moving integrity screening or peer-review operations in-house. The third is Education revenue falling year on year, excluding Unbound, in the second half of FY27. The fourth is Corporate Learning margin slipping back below 20% before it has returned to growth of about 12%.

book_paragraphs: Let me ask you something before we open a single table. If I told you that MPS turns scientists’ manuscripts into finished journal articles, builds eLearning for banks, and sells a nursing app to universities, would you call that one business or three? Most people say three. Management says one: a single engine of content, platforms and AI wearing three sets of clothes. You and I have to keep both ideas in our heads. The engine is shared, but the invoices are not, and the profit is certainly not. In FY26 the company reported revenue of about ₹768 crore. Research Solutions brought in ₹463.5 crore, roughly 60%. Education Solutions brought in ₹208.9 crore, 27%. Corporate Learning brought in ₹96 crore, about an eighth.

Now watch what happens when we follow the profit instead of the revenue. The audited segment note shows Research earning about two-thirds of the profit the segments report before corporate costs, Education about 30%, and Corporate Learning under 5%. So if someone describes MPS to you as a three-legged stool, gently correct them. It is one strong leg, one fast-growing leg whose newest piece is lower-margin, and one leg that is being rebuilt while we watch. That framing alone will protect you from a lot of conference-room enthusiasm.

Picture a scientist in Boston finishing a study. Her manuscript goes into a journal’s submission system. Somebody has to check it is not a paper-mill product, find two or three reviewers, chase them, collect the decisions, and then, if the paper is accepted, turn a Word file into a structured, typeset, accessible, searchable article that appears on a platform that thousands of libraries can reach. MPS touches almost every one of those steps for its publisher clients. It runs peer-review desks, it screens for fraud, it converts and composes the article, and through HighWire and DigiCore it can host the result. On the Q2 FY27 call, one of its research leaders said one of the five largest companies in the market is moving more than 110,000 submissions a year onto MPS’s peer-review platform. Rahul Arora, the chairman and CEO, put the customer’s problem in six words: ‘volume is not the issue, throughput is the issue.’

Here is where the AI story becomes real, and I want you to stay sceptical with me. In the old model a production vendor was paid by the page or the hour. If a tool saved you an hour, that was an hour you could no longer bill, and the customer would notice at renewal. Management says the model is shifting. In his words on the Q1 FY27 call: ‘Our revenue is steadily shifting from being paid for effort to being paid for outcomes.’ A submission screened, an article made ready, a title made accessible. If you price the finished unit, the saving from AI is shared between the customer and MPS rather than handed over in full. The CEO was candid about the split on the Q2 FY27 call: ‘Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume, and that’s where the margin kind of comes from.’

Is it working? The audited evidence says yes, with a caveat. Research employee cost fell from ₹185 crore to ₹160 crore in a year when the segment’s revenue was up only one percent, and the segment margin before corporate costs moved from about 37% to about 40%. In the first two quarters of FY27 management reported segment EBITDA margins of 45% and then 48%. The caveat is that part of the FY26 revenue flatness is AJE, the author-services business MPS bought from Springer Nature, which was deliberately shrunk. Excluding AJE, the annual report says Research grew about 17%. I like that the company took the pain in the reported number. I like it less that the 25% ‘outcome-based’ revenue share and the 45% ‘recurring’ share it quotes are not audited and not defined anywhere I can read.

Education is the segment that surprised everyone, and its story has two chapters. The first is the content and accessibility business: school publishers in the United States who need materials by a state adoption deadline, with accessible versions that the law requires. Revenue in this part has been lumpy. It grew 56% in the first quarter of FY26, 52% in the second, and then just 11% in the third, which the CEO called a one-off. The second chapter is Unbound Medicine, bought in February 2026 for US$16.5 million. Imagine a nurse on a night shift pulling out her phone to check a drug interaction. The reference she opens is licensed from names like Johns Hopkins and Oxford University Press, and her nursing school pays a yearly subscription. Unbound is about 35 people producing roughly US$9 million of revenue; its own release cites a 97% annual renewal rate; and the CEO says every renewal comes with a price increase.

That is a very different shape of revenue from a content project, and it comes with a price. Unbound’s margin is about 18 to 20%, up from 12 to 13% when MPS bought it, against project work that has run in the high thirties. That is the likeliest reason the first-half Education revenue grew 36% while its EBITDA grew only 14.5%. You and I should not read that as bad news. A recurring, price-escalating base is worth something that a project book never is. But you should know that growth in Education is no longer the same kind of growth that it was two years ago.

Then there is Corporate Learning, the repair job. Revenue fell from ₹115 crore to ₹96 crore, and the segment result nearly halved. Management responded by merging the businesses under one brand, Liberate Global, cutting headcount by about a third, and shifting to gig and associate delivery. The numbers since then are encouraging: a 25% margin in the first half of FY27 against about 16% a year earlier. But listen to how the segment head herself framed it: ‘This is not a recovery of the legacy business.’ She is telling you that what is being built is a different business, enterprise capability enablement, with AI-led programmes in place of course libraries. And the CEO admitted the market is growing at 12 to 13% while MPS grew 6 to 7. ‘That’s the area where a lot of the catch-up has to happen.’

Two more things belong in your mental picture. First, geography. About 43% of FY26 revenue came from US customers, 36% from Europe, and nearly 10% from China, which is all Research. Almost none came from India. Europe was the growth region, up 26%, while the United States was flat and China fell a quarter. Second, concentration. One customer accounted for 17.3% of group revenue, the top 15 for 58%, and the CFO told investors in November that the top five had fallen to 46%. That is improving. It is not yet comfortable, and in the next chapter you will see why that matters for how contracts are won and kept.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION: The honest shape of the profit pool
book_callouts.quote: Two-thirds of the profit sits in one segment, and two of the three segments are still being rebuilt.
book_callouts.text: When you sit across from a company that tells a clean three-segment story, ask which segment would be missed if it vanished tomorrow. For MPS the answer is Research Solutions by a wide margin. That does not make the other two unimportant. Education is the growth engine, and the Unbound subscription base is a genuinely new kind of revenue for this company. Corporate Learning is a turnaround whose cost fix is done and whose growth fix is still ahead.
bullets: Research: 60% of FY26 revenue and about 66% of segment profit; reported growth +1.0%, about +17% excluding AJE.
Education: 27% of revenue, +36% growth, 79% of it from US customers; first-half EBITDA grew slower than revenue as Unbound entered.
Corporate Learning: 12.5% of revenue, revenue -16.5%, segment margin 11.8%; first-half FY27 margin recovered to about 25%.

book_subsections.title: Walking a manuscript through the Research factory
paragraphs: I want you to follow one paper end to end, because abstractions about ‘content engineering’ do nothing for me. Step one is intake: the manuscript arrives in a peer-review system that MPS runs for the publisher. Step two is the integrity screen. MPS says its Research Integrity Check sits on top of its DigiCore production platform and looks for paper-mill fingerprints, identity fraud and doctored images. Step three is people: editors and reviewers are found, nudged and chased, and decisions are logged. This is the journal editorial office work that management says scaled because of the AJE deal.

Step four is the factory proper. An accepted paper is converted into structured files, composed into the journal’s layout, checked, and sent for author proofs. On MPS’s own description, its tools automate composition and run quality checks before the proofs ever reach a human; on the Q1 FY27 call they described one-touch workflows and automated alt-text for accessibility. The finished article is then published on a hosting platform, often HighWire, the Stanford-born platform MPS bought in 2020. The customer’s view is a dashboard and a clean article. MPS’s view is a unit of work that used to need many touches and now needs fewer.

Why does the customer pay on the outcome rather than the hours? Because the customer’s real problem is throughput. When a publisher is drowning in submissions, an extra day’s delay costs more than a small price difference, and the vendor that clears the queue gets more volume, which is exactly the loop the CEO described.

book_subsections.title: A nursing school, a state adoption and a bank: three customers, three invoices
paragraphs: Each segment sends a very different invoice. The nursing school gets a once-a-year subscription invoice for Unbound’s Nursing Central, with an escalator built in, billed in advance. When MPS bought Unbound it inherited about ₹35 crore of deferred revenue on that basis. The state-adoption publisher gets milestone invoices for a project, recognised as work is completed, with the economics decided by how many hours AI took out of the build. The Australian bank, the archetype for Liberate’s clients, gets a fixed-price programme or a managed-service fee for modernising thousands of legacy courses into role-based, AI-assisted learning.

Notice what these have in common and what they do not. All three customers are mostly outside India; all three purchase something that is hard to build and easy to verify; all three have reasons to ask for lower prices now that AI exists. What they do not share is the revenue shape. One is annuity-like, one is lumpy and calendar-driven, and one is project-based and rebuilding. If you want to forecast this company, you will need three separate mental models.

There is a human point here too. The same company that sells a subscription to a nursing school employs, in Research, more than two thousand people who chase reviewers and check proofs, and in Corporate Learning well under three hundred designers and developers whose work is increasingly flexed through freelancers. Different invoices mean different workforces, different attrition problems and different ways for a bad quarter to show up. When a call tells you that headcount is ‘stable’, ask which segment it is stable in.

book_subsections.title: What AI-first does and does not change
paragraphs: The annual report says the company’s advantage is ‘not access to models, which everyone has’ but proprietary content and domain context. I find that credible for Unbound, where the licensed medical content is the moat. I find it more mixed for Research, where Springer Nature has built its own detector for AI-generated nonsense text and donated it to an industry hub, and where COPE, the publication-ethics body, records that no AI detector is fully accurate. In both cases MPS’s better argument is the workflow, not the detection.

So here is how I would summarise AI in this chapter without cheerleading. It has already lowered MPS’s cost per unit of work, and the audited segment note shows it. It has not yet been tested through a hard price reset with a large customer, because the biggest contracts run three to five years and were won on a throughput story. The evidence we need is the next big renewal: whether the customer keeps the gains or MPS does.

One more honest observation. The company’s own letter to shareholders says generative AI threatens ‘business models built on undifferentiated content production’, and that MPS is positioned in verification, workflow orchestration and trusted distribution. Notice the quiet admission inside that sentence: a good part of MPS’s historical revenue was content production. The strategy is therefore a migration, from the part of the value chain that AI cheapens to the part it makes scarce. The numbers say the migration has begun; they do not yet say it is finished.
